'''Boyd Eugene Haley''' (born September 22, 1940,{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}} [[Greensburg, Indiana]]) is an American [[Anti-vaccine activism|anti-vaccine activist]] and retired professor of chemistry at the [[University of Kentucky]].

==Education and career==
A native of [[Greensburg, Indiana]], Haley graduated from its New Point High School in 1959. Four years later, he received a bachelor's degree from [[Franklin College (Indiana)|Franklin College]] in [[Franklin, Indiana]], and then entered a teaching fellowship at [[Howard University]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/15065515/ |title=Boyd Eugene Haley |website=Greensburg Daily News |date=13 June 1963}}</ref>  Thereafter, he served as a U.S. Army medic for several years.

In 1967, Haley obtained an M.S. degree from the [[University of Idaho]]. He then entered a doctoral program at Washington State University, where he worked "to make chemical modifications on ATP to try to identify how and exactly where ATP binds to cause muscle movement."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.research.uky.edu/odyssey/exclusive/summer03/haley.html|title=Boyd Haley: Tagging toxins for better health|publisher=[[University of Kentucky]]|date=25 September 2003|access-date=7 October 2013|author=Worley, Jeff|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141113004443/http://www.research.uky.edu/odyssey/exclusive/summer03/haley.html|archive-date=13 November 2014}}</ref> In 1971, WSU granted him his Ph.D. degree in chemistry-biochemistry.

For three years, Haley served as a postdoctoral scholar at [[Yale University]]. From 1974 to 1985, he was a professor at the [[University of Wyoming]].<ref name=FDA/>  hereafter, he was appointed professor of medicinal chemistry at the University of Kentucky, whose chemistry department he became chairperson of in 1997.<ref name=FDA/> He is now{{As of?|date=July 2026}} [[professor emeritus]].<ref>[https://chem.as.uky.edu/adjunct-emeritus-faculty "Adjunct & emeritus faculty"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171009195814/https://chem.as.uky.edu/adjunct-emeritus-faculty |date=2017-10-09 }}, College of Arts & Sciences—Chemistry wepbage, University of Kentucky website, accessed 13 Jun 2017.</ref>

==Basic research==

In 1992, Haley and a colleague, upon examining [[cerebrospinal fluid]], reported levels of [[glutamine synthetase]] considerably higher in cases of [[Alzheimer's disease]] than in a [[control group]], and suggested that this could be a biomarker to aid diagnosis.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Gunnersen D, Haley B|title=Detection of glutamine synthetase in the cerebrospinal fluid of Alzheimer diseased patients: A potential diagnostic biochemical marker|journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A.|volume=89|issue=24|pages=11949–53|date=December 1992|pmid=1361232|pmc=50675|doi=10.1073/pnas.89.24.11949|bibcode=1992PNAS...8911949G|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/12/15/news/a-possible-alzheimer-marker-is-found.html|title=A possible Alzheimer marker is found|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=15 December 1992|access-date=12 February 2014}}</ref>

In 2005, Haley reproduced findings of gold salt removing mercury from molecules, and inferred support for the possibility of gold salts removing mercury from biological proteins.<ref name=Olmsted/>  Yet Haley noted that the gold salts could themselves be toxic, and called for the extreme caution before applying gold salts in medical treatment.<ref name=Olmsted>{{cite news|url=http://www.upi.com/Consumer_Health_Daily/Reports/2005/12/30/the_age_of_autism_gold_standards/2870/|title=The Age of Autism: Gold standards|publisher=[[United Press International]]|date=2005-12-30|access-date=2008-01-04|last=Olmsted|first=Dan|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080320060501/http://www.upi.com/NewsTrack/Health/2005/12/30/the_age_of_autism_gold_standards/2870/|archive-date=20 March 2008}}</ref>

==Thimerosal controversy==
{{further|Dental amalgam controversy}}

Haley argues that mercury exposure via dental [[amalgam (dentistry)|amalgams]] and vaccinations may cause neurological impairments and diseases, such as [[autism]] and [[Alzheimer's disease]].<ref>Rockmarch, Andrea. (April 2004). "[https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2011/02/toxic-tipping-point/ Toxic Tipping Point]", ''[[Mother Jones (magazine)|Mother Jones]]''. Retrieved August 26, 2018.</ref> The [[United States Public Health Service]] and the [[American Dental Association]] reject these claims.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.fda.gov/cdrh/consumer/amalgams.html|title=Questions and Answers on Dental Amalgam|date=2006-10-30|access-date=2008-01-04|publisher=[[Food and Drug Administration]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071019060424/https://www.fda.gov/cdrh/consumer/amalgams.html|archive-date=2007-10-19|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ada.org/prof/resources/positions/statements/amalgam.asp|title=ADA Statement on Dental Amalgam|date=2007-04-06|access-date=2008-01-04|publisher=[[American Dental Association]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071011130327/http://ada.org/prof/resources/positions/statements/amalgam.asp|archive-date=2007-10-11|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Haley has appeared in court as an expert witness against vaccine manufacturers, stating his belief that [[thimerosal]] causes autism, but his testimony has not been accepted.<ref name=prophets>{{cite book |author=Offit PA |publisher=Columbia University Press |chapter=Behind the Mercury Curtain |title=Autism's False Prophets: Bad Science, Risky Medicine, and the Search for a Cure |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=er6rAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA132 |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-231-14637-1 |pages=132–133}}</ref> In 2008 a judge ruled that his "lack of expertise in genetics, epidemiology, and child neurology make it impossible for him to supply the necessary factual basis to support his testimony".<ref name=prophets/>

Haley has labeled autism as "mad child disease" (akin to [[mad cow disease]]), which many autistic individuals and their parents have found highly offensive.<ref name="Offit2010">{{cite book|author=Paul A. Offit|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=er6rAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA132|title=Autism's False Prophets: Bad Science, Risky Medicine, and the Search for a Cure|date=2 April 2010|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=978-0-231-14637-1|page=132}}</ref><ref name="Dignity">{{cite web|date=July 2005|title=Petition to Defend the Dignity of Autistic Citizens|url=http://www.neurodiversity.com/mothers_for_dignity.html|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927224839/http://www.neurodiversity.com/mothers_for_dignity.html|archive-date=27 September 2007|access-date=2007-11-07|publisher=neurodiversity.com}}</ref>

==Supplement marketing==
Haley is the founder of CTI Science, a [[Lexington, Kentucky]]-based biotechnology firm. CTI marketed a product, [[BDTH2|OSR#1]], for human consumption; it was described as an "antioxidant" [[dietary supplement]] that is a powerful [[Chelation therapy|chelator]] from a family originally developed to remove [[heavy metal (chemistry)|heavy metals]] from soil and [[acid mine drainage]].<ref name=Trib>[http://www.chicagotribune.com/health/chi-autism-chemicaljan17,0,6466364.story "OSR#1: Industrial chemical or autism treatment?"], ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'', January 17, 2010</ref>  In June 2008, an FDA toxicologist questioned<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20100726073800/https://www.regulations.gov/search/Regs/contentStreamer?objectId=09000064806d97e6&disposition=attachment&contentType=pdf FDA letters and documents]</ref> "on what basis the product could be expected to be safe and could be considered a dietary ingredient", but CTI Science and Haley had not responded as of January 2010.<ref name=Trib/> The testing was described as incomplete and indicating toxicity.<ref>{{cite news|title=FDA warns maker of autism supplement|url=http://www.upi.com/Health_News/2010/06/24/FDA-warns-maker-of-autism-supplement/UPI-44231277415294/|work=UPI|date=June 24, 2010|access-date=September 12, 2011}}</ref> On June 17, 2010, the FDA sent a [[FDA Warning Letter|warning letter]] noting five potential violations, expressing concern over the testing, and requiring a response in 15 days.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20100626070849/http://www.fda.gov/ICECI/EnforcementActions/WarningLetters/ucm216216.htm Warning letter CIN-10-107927-14] from [[Food and Drug Administration|US FDA]], June 17, 2010</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=FDA warns maker of product used as alternative autism treatment|first=Trine|last=Tsouderos|author-link=Trine Tsouderos|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2010/06/23/fda-warns-maker-of-product-used-as-alternative-autism-treatment/|newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]]|issn=1085-6706|date=June 23, 2010|access-date=September 12, 2011}}</ref> Although Haley wrote an [[op-ed]] for the ''[[Lexington Herald-Leader]]'',<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.kentucky.com/2010/07/12/1345487/dietary-supplement-safe-for-right.html|title=Dietary supplement safe for right use|last=Haley|first=Boyd|date=June 26, 2010|newspaper=[[Lexington Herald-Leader]]|access-date=September 12, 2011|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120904220818/http://www.kentucky.com/2010/07/12/1345487/dietary-supplement-safe-for-right.html|archive-date=September 4, 2012|url-status=dead|issn=0745-4260}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Supplement seller says FDA may be 'confused'|first=Trine|last=Tsouderos|author-link=Trine Tsouderos|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2010/07/12/supplement-seller-says-fda-may-be-confused/|newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]]|issn=1085-6706|date=July 12, 2010|access-date=September 12, 2011}}</ref> the FDA did not receive a formal response, and OSR#1 was withdrawn from the market.<ref>{{cite news|title=Controversial supplement to come off shelves|first=Trine|last=Tsouderos|author-link=Trine Tsouderos|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2010/07/26/controversial-supplement-to-come-off-shelves/|newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]]|issn=1085-6706|date=July 26, 2010|access-date=September 12, 2011}}</ref> In July 2014, CTI Science was acquired by [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]]-based EmeraMed Limited, which rebranded Haley's antioxidant/chelator as Emeramide and, as of 2026, is still seeking regulatory approval for the drug in the United States, the [[European Union]], and [[South America]].<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date= |title=CTI Science — Company Profile |url=https://www.thecompanycheck.com/company/b/cti-science/o7lhf0lvl3xwcmahy |access-date=2026-07-15 |website=The Company Check |language=en-IN}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=About EmeraMed |url=https://emeramed.com/about/ |access-date=2026-07-15 |website=EmeraMed |language=en-US}}</ref> As of 2026, Haley is EmeraMed's [[chief scientific officer|chief scientist]] and [[CEO]].<ref name=":0" />
